items.question: Why did you see language processing as a promising way to study cognition?
items.object: Language processing as a way to study cognition
items.answer: To the extent that I think what I've always been interested in is thought, it felt like these deeper questions about cognition and how you build artificial models of cognition were closer to the surface in language processing and language understanding problems than at least in what was going on at the time in vision and robotics and things like that. I'm sure people in the vision world would disagree with that, and I think this was a pretty widespread view in NLP that was not a widespread view in the rest of the AI world. It seems to have actually borne out pretty well in terms of it being language models that got us into the state that we are right now.

items.question: What kinds of research tasks do you consider important when studying language as a window into cognition?
items.object: Research tasks for studying language as a window into cognition
items.answer: As soon as you start saying, "I'm really interested in language as a window into cognition," the kinds of tasks that seem important to study are not just language processing tasks as we typically think about them, part of speech tags and parse trees and even summarization. It's about building systems that act in the real world and relate language to external things, to actions that they take, to things that they can perceive. I remember being really inspired by a lot of the work that Branavan and Regina Barzilay were doing right here at MIT, and at the same time Ray Mooney and a bunch of his students at UT, doing some of the first really exciting work thinking about how to relate language to perception and action.

items.question: How has your view changed about whether learning from text alone requires explicit grounding to produce an understanding of the world?
items.object: Grounding fundamentalism and learning about the world from text
items.answer:
The important thing at the time was that it felt totally implausible that you could, from text alone, learn how to do any of that, or that you could from text alone learn enough about how the outside world worked that you would wind up with a copy of or a model of the outside world inside the parameters of one of these models just by doing anything with text, to say nothing of just doing next word prediction. To the extent that I was a grounding fundamentalist, it was that we have all of these tasks that we care about that are clearly not about understanding language as such, but about understanding the rest of the world. With the kinds of models and learning algorithms that we had access to in 2012, 2013, 2014, it felt unlikely or maybe even impossible that we would be able to learn all of those deeper things about meaning without some explicit evidence for the way in which language related to the outside world.

The big thing there is we underestimated, or at least I underestimated, just how much there actually is once you start talking about internet scale text corpora. There are still a lot of important questions about what you can do with a sort of humanized text corpus as opposed to an internet sized text corpus, but once we have access to and the ability to train on internet sized text corpora, it turns out that a lot of the things that we thought you couldn't get from language, you can after all.

items.question: How did you assess GPT-2’s early long-form text generation in the context of the language models that preceded it?
items.object: GPT-2's early long-form text generation
items.answer: Well, yeah, I mean, certainly I was one of the people saying, “Oh my, I didn't expect that,” at least even with GPT-2 and the first long-form text generation that was coming out of GPT-2, which now we look back at it and say, “Oh, this is garbage. items.question: How do you now understand the relationship between syntactic parsing and understanding the world?
items.object: Part-of-speech tagging and syntactic parsing as tests of language understanding
items.answer:
I was saying things like part of speech tagging and parsing don't really get at language understanding. But in fact they were, right? The kinds of mistakes that syntactic constituency parsers on the Penn Treebank were making, even really when I started grad school in 2013, when we were starting to do latent variable models and representation learning, in many cases had to do with understanding the world and not understanding the rules of English.

It wasn't like, is this thing a prepositional phrase or not? But is it more plausible that, if I have potatoes in a bag on the back of a truck, the potatoes are in the bag or basically where the bag is with respect to the back of the truck? Because it felt intractable to make progress on those problems with the kinds of data sets we had access to, I feel like we were looking at them and saying, where is the information about the conventional relationship between the potatoes and the bag and the truck going to come from? It's not going to be text corpora, because every individual one of those situations you're going to have to learn a model of from scratch, and you just aren't going to see all the necessary co-occurrence statistics. The way in which we're doing this is imagining how that scene plays out in our head, and surely to do that you have to have actually seen some of all of these objects in the first place.

items.question: What do you find surprising about language models learning about the outside world from text alone?
items.object: Learning models of the outside world from text alone
items.answer:
I think that's basically where I was when all this language modeling stuff started indicating that it was moving in the direction of working as well as it was going to. You could say, “Here's a statistical pattern that governs the distribution of well-formed text documents. We're not getting it when we're just training on text data, so clearly you must need some other source of information to model the world.” What has actually wound up being the case is, precisely because the world constrains the set of text documents that you can produce, and we can see effectively all of the text documents, you can back out and practice the constraints that exist on the world. I found that very surprising, and even though I've gotten used to it and it's a big part of our research, I still find it incredibly surprising that this turns out to be the case.

Talking about commitments, it's always been the case, and I think for large parts of the community it's always been the case, that we've understood language is an image of the outside world in some way, and therefore being able to build good models of language-intrinsic properties at some level requires being able to build models of the outside world. The surprising thing was not that that turns out to be true, but just that the kind of data you need to learn that model of the outside world, perhaps not in the most efficient way possible but in the most practical way possible, may not go through any outside world at all.

items.question: How do you think meaning should be defined to make grounding in language models an interesting scientific question?
items.object: Definitions of meaning and grounding for language models
items.answer:
I guess the naive thing to say here is that it doesn't feel like there's actually a very deep philosophical problem here. There are a few different ways in which you can formalize this, and there is deep philosophy behind all of this, but it's all pre-existing. You can say a word derives its meaning from social context, from a history of use, and then there are lots of things you can say about the causal relationship between human societies and the documents that they produce, and then the knowledge language models acquire from those documents. If you have this causal theory of meaning, I think that's satisfied by current models.

You can take the attitude that to understand the meaning of a word requires really directly being able to ground that thing in perception, that there needs to be some direct correspondence between what it feels like qualitatively to perceive the color blue and the word blue. If you stipulate that, obviously the kinds of models we're training on text data, and maybe even the kinds of models we're training on perceptual data that's filtered not through human eyes but through other kinds of sensors, don't satisfy that property. We can say without doing any experiments ahead of time that models will never understand meaning in this sense. This is true, but I think it's maybe not a useful or interesting definition.

Then you can say to know the meaning of a word is to relate it to some broader conceptual model of how the world works, and it's enough for that model to be isomorphic to what exists outside in the real world or to the thing that exists in other people's heads. I think most mathematically inclined people have the intuition that objects that are the same up to a unique isomorphism are just the same. If you take that perspective, then you have an interesting empirical question: under what conditions do models trained on very different kinds of data from the models people are trained on acquire a representation that's isomorphic, or sort of isomorphic, in particular bits and pieces, to the things that exist in our head or in the real world? I think that's kind of where we are right now. You can define meaning or understanding in all of these different ways, but the one that gives rise to an interesting scientific question or engineering problem is the one that says, for grounding, it's enough to have a representation that's isomorphic to the real world.

items.question: Why do you see language models as scientifically interesting even apart from their practical usefulness?
items.object: The scientific value of studying language models
items.answer:
One thing I'm interested in is the science of models that look like language models. The things that LLMs and related technologies have been able to do turned out to be quite surprising, not just to people working in machine learning and NLP, but also to people studying intelligence and other kinds of biological systems, people interested in complex systems generally, and people interested in large-scale data-driven methods applied not just to language.

There's something to understand here, something deep scientifically to say about the conditions under which you learn structured representations of the world, learn how to learn, learn reasoning procedures, what kinds of data you need, and what kinds of predictive models you need. Even if there were zero economic or practical value in producing these things, those would be really interesting and important questions. They're not directly about human intelligence or biological intelligence, but about the kinds of things you can learn from large amounts of the right kind of data and the things you can do to build intelligence systems generally. That's where all of these questions about what the internal representations in these models look like and under what conditions they assume particular forms are important.

items.question: How do you assess what current language models can teach you about human intelligence?
items.object: Language models as explanations of human intelligence and the role of grounding
items.answer:
What's tricky is that there was this beautiful period when it seemed like all three of these questions were going to have the same set of answers: how do you build an AI system useful to people, understand the conditions under which intelligence-seeming behavior arises, and explain why human intelligence specifically looks the way it does? They all seemed to require a common set of tools or questions. We were going to think deeply about how our own intelligence worked, replicate that in silico, and wind up with these really useful things.

That turned out not to be the world we live in. We have ways of building incredibly interesting and in some cases incredibly useful language technologies in ways that I think actually teach us very little about how human intelligence works, at least naively applied. The fundamental issue is that we learn not from internet-scale data but from much, much smaller amounts of language data, and we currently have no way of training computational models from scratch on the same kinds of data and getting them to human-level performance on these tasks. I would be surprised if, when we have models able to do that, those things will look very much at all like modern language models, or if there won't be some other important piece of that system that we haven't yet discovered.

The behaviors you exhibit as a competent adult human are the result of two nested optimization processes: the optimization process that you as a learner are solving over your lifetime, and the optimization process Evolution is solving on an evolutionary timescale. Evolution, to a first approximation, has never seen a language; it definitely has not seen English. To the extent that you're able to acquire adult-like English capabilities from tiny amounts of data, it's because there's something special about the place that the evolutionary optimizer put you in, in virtue of which you're able to learn English. I just don't think we're learning very much about what that initialization looks like from training models on language from day one in a way that, from start to end, looks very different from the kinds of data a human learner gets.

Maybe there's some very clever meta-learning thing you can do, such that given all the data a human is going to see in their lifetime, a model trained on the same data—and maybe only the language part of that data—learns to do the same thing. It seems much more plausible that all the stuff about grounding and perception and social context, being able to take action in the world and do experiments, is really essential for answering these scientific questions about how intelligence works. It's less clear to me that those things are still on the critical path towards building useful technologies, at least in the present.

items.question: How do you assess the analogy between language-model pretraining and human learning?
items.object: The analogy between language-model pretraining and human learning
items.answer:
I don't want to suggest that there's no analogy at all to draw between what, at least at the behavioral level, a language model is doing and aspects of what's going on in human learning. There's robust evidence at this point that human infants can do statistical learning in these kinds of sequence-processing tasks from a very, very young age, and that some amount of prediction or predictive coding is pretty central to how we learn and what we think of as intelligent behavior in humans.

Maybe the distinction I'm trying to draw is between saying prediction generically teaches you a lot about the world and is a useful supervisory signal if you're going to build some sort of intelligence system, and saying that specifically the prediction problem we use for pretraining current language models in any fine-grained way looks like the prediction problem we use for training, or that is going on in the course of human learning.

One other subtlety: it's not clear to me how much this is a language-specific distinction. People in the vision world have made the corresponding observation that representations in visual models, or representations in computer vision models trained on computer vision tasks, look a lot like or align well to visual representations in the human brain. Circuits that show up in early vision also show up in circuits for the lowest layers of these models. We can make the same observations about representations of language in the human brain and representations of language in language models, although exactly what we're finding correspondences between seems a little less clear. I think you can certainly draw a coarse analogy between predictive coding being important in language models and important in people, but the really deeper, interesting question about people is: what is that inductive bias that we are born with that allows us to learn language and all the other things we do from orders of magnitude less data than the models we're training right now? Any answer to that question needs to explain how you get there without the thing that produces that initializer having already seen all of the adult-like capabilities you're eventually going to acquire. We're not really learning much about that from training models on “adult-like” capabilities.

items.question: What would you find satisfying in an explanation of how evolution equipped humans to learn language?
items.object: Evolutionary origins of human language-learning abilities
items.answer: I think it is at least not at all obvious that a satisfying answer to “What did evolution give us?” should be able to say anything about language at all. It would be much nicer if you could say, and this is the dream: here's some family of environments or some distribution over learning problems that are not exactly language learning problems, such that if you have a really good meta-learner for this distribution over learning problems, then if you present language learning as the N-plus-first learning problem, you can do that with human-like abilities. items.question: How did you want to change the way formal semantic approaches connected language to the world?
items.object: Grounding language through executable meaning representations with learned execution semantics
items.answer:
There had been a bunch of work in the NLP world from Ray Mooney and colleagues, from Luke Zettlemoyer and Collins, and from Yoav Artzi, who was Luke Zettlemoyer's student, on mapping and parsing language into formal representations of meaning that, to a computer scientist, look like little programs in the lambda calculus. Because those things are programs, you can execute them against some sort of representation of the real world. What felt like it was missing was that all the work up to that point said, “Once you've got the program, you're all done. The execution semantics is known to you ahead of time. I can promise you there's some concept in your formal language called purple or dog, such that if you can learn the mapping from the word dog to the program name dog in your programming language, you'll be able to do all of language understanding.”

This notion that you need to have the language of thought, the language in which all of your meaning representations are expressed, available to you ahead of time in order for language to have something to latch on to is a very old one. You were mentioning the symbol grounding paper before; this is also very much in Jerry Fodor's work. With the hubris of a first-year grad student, it felt like we could do better and relax the assumption that we had access to the language of thought, if you want to call it that. We could instead try to translate language into executable representations where the execution semantics itself was learned end to end with everything else. We did a very shallow version of that in that paper, but I think that was the driving idea behind a lot of my PhD work: how do you, in what we would now call an end-to-end way, learn how to go from language directly to perception or directly to action without passing through some intermediate structured representation of meaning or thought that already told you how the world works or what the important concepts were?

It started in that paper, and then we had a follow-up paper in a very similar spirit on instruction following, trying to do instruction following without formal semantics. Some of the Branavan work had done that before, but people had mostly moved away from it toward these more formal semantics models. The whole line of ModuleNets papers was really the culmination of that: what does it look like to do structured computation on the world conditional on language, where nobody's told you ahead of time what the primitive elements of computation are?

items.question: How do you assess the structural assumptions you imposed on the world in your early work on grounding language in perception and action?
items.object: Structural assumptions about events in early models of language grounding
items.answer:
For a little context, if I remember right—you may have read this paper more recently than I have—there's just learning grounding of color, compositional color terms; there's a problem where we're trying to predict stock market trajectories from Wall Street headlines or something like that, where there's some squishy, continuously parameterized thing that's being described in language and you want to try to recover it; and then something that looks more like a standard instruction-following task.

We do this by saying each of these things, whether it's a color or a trajectory in space or a trajectory in some abstract feature space, I'm going to think of as consisting of a sequence of events. The events have parameters, and I'm going to learn some sparse model that tries to sparsely associate words with events and features of those events. If the question is how much you can learn about how language grounds out in these relatively low-level percepts or actions, it would be nice to assume as little structure in the world as possible. The standard thing in NLP at the time was to say, “I'm going to have some programming language that allows me to generate these colors or shapes directly,” and typically those programming languages were informed by what we already knew about natural language, with a pretty nice one-to-one correspondence between formal operators and words in language.

This was saying, what's the minimal structure you can assume in your representation of the world? I would have loved to get all the way to literally just a sequence of points in your high-dimensional representation space without any additional structure superimposed on top of those. But with the tools we had then and the skills I had as a first-year grad student, we needed to impose a little bit of structure. There, I think, is legitimately some cognitive science you can appeal to for why those are the right structural assumptions to make. Now I think we could say more interesting things about the special and core knowledge that shapes your representations of these things, but truthfully, it was more because that's what we had to do to get the learning to work.

items.question: How do you assess your 2014 paper on using word embeddings for syntactic prediction in hindsight?
items.object: His 2014 paper on word embeddings for syntactic prediction
items.answer:
That was a paper where word embeddings were the new hot thing, and they were used for all kinds of classification tasks. It wasn't yet clear whether they were going to be useful for more structured prediction things. We had a really good parser lying around at Berkeley, and could we use these word embeddings to make it better? The conclusion was basically no.

I agree that's a very nice, clean, well-designed paper. The most important thing about it is it was completely wrong in terms of whether word embeddings or these kinds of continuous representations were useful for doing any kind of syntactic prediction. The work that Richard Socher and D. I think, on one hand, that was a really good, useful early experience of saying, “Hey, we have this question,” getting a bunch of negative results. items.question: How has your experience with neural parsing changed your view of how much structure you need to build into a machine learning model?
items.object: Built-in structure versus learning from data in machine learning
items.answer:
I think, in retrospect, the big lesson there, and one that actually took me a very long time to learn, is just to not be too tied to the best model that you happen to have lying around today, and to not underestimate the ability of very simple statistical methods trained on large amounts of data to figure out how to do the things your fancy structured method can do on its own. Obviously, this is in some sense the entire lesson, or at least large parts of the ML community went through a version of it in the last decade.

I very distinctly remember the first AlexNet paper came out, the vision people were all freaking out, and we were sitting two bays over patting ourselves on the back, saying, “Oh yes, this neural stuff is very nice, but it will never do any kind of structured output.” Then all the sequence-to-sequence papers happened, and we didn't freak out. We said, “This is very nice, but it'll never do trees and graphs and other objects with combinatorial structure that's not just sequences.” In fact, they didn't, but the best way to get a tree-shaped thing was just to linearize the tree and then do sequence prediction on top of the tree. Thinking about structured potentials that allow you to place probability distributions over well-formed constituency trees was entirely the wrong way of thinking about this problem, not because constituency syntax isn't real in some way, but because it doesn't play nicely with the machine learning tools that work.

We went down a whole path of trying to figure out how to take existing parsing machinery and make it play nicely with these neural representations. This paper we've been talking about was a negative result. David Hall and Greg Durrett, and later Nikita Kitaev and Mitchell Stern, and the group I was in in grad school, subsequently had a bunch of really successful neural structured prediction things, and that just wound up not being on the critical path at all. I think that's a version in miniature of this larger conversation about what you learn about the world and how much prior structure you need to build in about how the world works or the link between perception and action. The lesson of the last few years has always been less than we thought.

items.question: How did studying neural sequence models trained on regular-language data change your understanding of the computations they learn?
items.object: The computations neural sequence models learn from regular-language data
items.answer:
We were convinced that when we trained neural sequence models on large amounts of this data, they would somehow recapitulate internally the classical learning algorithm for recovering a finite state automaton from observations of that thing.

The attention heads weren't really behaving in a way consistent with this, and the predictions from the models weren't really behaving in a way consistent with this. Eventually I realized that the model was learning to do something much simpler: it was not solving this fancy latent-variable problem at all; it was just learning to be a little n-gram model. This is a very literal example of what we're talking about. We probably would have been able to finish this project faster had we had weaker assumptions going in about the form of the computation the model was performing. In fact, it wound up being something not quite like a classical n-gram model, because there's some nice learned smoothing you can do on top of it. It also very much wound up not looking like a classical DFA induction algorithm.

items.question: How do you understand the evolution of your research from your PhD work on ModuleNet to the questions your lab pursues today?
items.object: The evolution of Jacob Andreas’s research from ModuleNet toward model-agnostic interpretability and supervision
items.answer:
It's interesting: my big PhD line of work was the ModuleNet stuff, which I think has not stood the test of time all that well, but led to some other questions about interpretability that informed the shape of the work the lab here is doing today. Some of these questions about language as an intermediate representation for computation, or as something that can supervise representations you're using for other tasks outside that specific module in that framework, are still very much what we're thinking about these days.

You have to go through this exercise of differentiating yourself a little bit, not even necessarily from your grad school lab, but from your own grad school work, and say, “Hey, I have a research direction that's longer than five years and can have room for more than just me inside it.” Coming off the ModuleNet stuff, what I was excited about was basically interpretability and rich supervision in a more model-agnostic way, because by then I was finally starting to see the light about the usefulness of architecture hacking as opposed to other things. I think that's where the “Measuring Compositionality” paper came from, where the “Learning with Latent Language” paper came from, the last thing I did on campus, and the translating neurons, the first real form of automated interpretability. Those were the last three slides of my job talk and are kind of what the lab has wound up working on.

items.question: How has your understanding of who sets a research lab’s agenda changed since you became a principal investigator?
items.object: How research agendas emerge within academic labs
items.answer:
Something I didn't totally appreciate then but have come to appreciate more now is that you think maybe as a grad student that the PI is running the show, or that there is such a thing as the direction for the lab and you're in the lab because you're interested in that direction. In fact, it's entirely the other direction: the grad students are setting the agenda when you're starting out as a new PI. items.question: How did you arrive at the beliefs, desires, and intentions framing in your position paper “Language Models as Agent Models”?
items.object: The argument behind “Language Models as Agent Models”
items.answer:
Well, this was, on one hand, my attempt to reconcile myself with all the stuff that was going on in LLM land and do some of the work of causing myself to not be surprised by what was going to happen in the future.

On the other hand, my student Belinda Lee had shortly before that had a paper at ACL on trying to figure out the structure of state representations inside what were then the kinds of models we could do experiments with, which were tiny, like BART/T5-size things. They found evidence for crude—and in retrospect, even cruder than we realized at the time—information about the states of entities and relationships between entities being mentioned in a discourse, and a little bit of information about where those things were located and what properties those things had. There was a nice follow-up paper by Sebastian Schuster and Naun Kim a little bit later finding that in fact things were probably even messier than we originally thought.

On one hand, this was evidence that models were in some way representing the state of the world internally, but not in any way perfectly isomorphic to the real world, just something. A natural question is: if models are representing states of entities in a discourse, what other kinds of things might they be representing? More abstractly, what kinds of things might be useful to have inside your representations if you're going to do a really good job of modeling the entire distribution over documents generated by human authors?

I think that leads you pretty naturally to this beliefs, desires, intentions model. Once you have that as a framing device, we could find in the literature similarly crude representations of desires or communicative intentions, either behaviorally or representationally in models at the time. But I think that was more speculative than descriptive: an attempt to not be surprised by what future versions of these models were going to be capable of.

items.question: How do you see ChatGPT’s emergence in relation to the argument in your position paper “Language Models as Agent Models”?
items.object: ChatGPT’s relationship to the models described in “Language Models as Agent Models”
items.answer: One really interesting thing is that between submitting that paper to EMNLP and the paper actually getting in, ChatGPT came out. In some ways, that was very much in line with what was being claimed in the paper, in the sense that now you have this system very explicitly designed to be agentic and to act as though it has a coherent set of goals and a coherent personality or whatever. On the other hand, it's a very different kind of model from the language models I was talking about in that position paper. It's no longer a model of the distribution over everything on the internet. It no longer really needs the ability to infer what the author at the beginning of a document was trying to accomplish in order to do the best job of completing that document at the end. In some ways, the world became much more interesting after that paper was written, because we now have, on one hand, models that look like the models I was talking about there, which are models of the entire internet, and, on the other hand, tools—which don't always work all that well—that are intended to convert these models of the internet into models not of the mixture of all agents, but of one specifically.

items.question: How has your view of the role of toy and synthetic experiments in understanding large language models changed?
items.object: Toy and synthetic experiments in language-model interpretability research
items.answer:
I could talk for another hour about toy experiments and the role of toy experiments in interpretability research. When I was starting out, there was a real aversion to anything that looked like a block world. Even some of the natural data sets but relatively simple grounding I was looking at in early grad school, reviewers often reacted extremely negatively to. It was kind of known in the NLP world that if you have a toy synthetic data set and you're just evaluating the performance of your nice structured model on it, you're going to do great, and you may not have produced a model useful at all in the real world.

Now we're in this weird other place where we have big language models, we know they work well at everything—not everything, but they do something sensible for basically whatever problem you want to throw at them—and we just want to understand how. I was very skeptical for a long time that we could learn anything about these big models and what happens when you train on the entire internet by looking at representations in models trained on toy data. I think that has not turned out to be true at all, and there's a lot of high-quality interpretability work that generalizes to large-scale data, or descriptions of large-scale models, that starts from toy experiments.

Even in that Lee et al. paper, we had a version with a pre-existing natural data set, with human beings writing down instructions for a little beaker manipulation task, and then a synthetic version of the same task. The representations look the same; the interventions seem to have similar effects. I think how I think about the role of synthetic experiments has changed a lot in the last five years. That being said, the experiments in the “Language Models as Agent Models” paper are very, very simple, and, as you're saying, I think not convincing on their own that you definitely expect much bigger models trained on much more complicated data distributions to encode much more complicated things in their hidden representations. Now that we have a clear picture of what those things might be, there are better, more interesting versions of those experiments that one could and should do.

items.question: Why do you think synthetic data is important for evaluating the capabilities of models pretrained on the entire internet?

items.answer: Well, I think the salient difference is, first of all, for evaluating capabilities of models, especially models pretrained on the entire internet, you almost need synthetic data rather than natural data, so that whatever biases in the natural data distribution the model may have hooked into aren't present, and you can make sure you're actually evaluating what you're evaluating behaviorally. That was a big shift.

I think this is more of an inductive claim than anything else, but it seems to be the case that often when we figure out how some phenomenon works in a small model and then look at a bigger model, it works the same: the encoding happens in the same place, in the same way. items.question: In what sense do you think word embedding models such as Word2Vec can have world models?
items.object: Word2Vec and word embeddings as world models
items.answer:
I think people actually mean a lot of different and mutually incompatible things with that term. I think there are even interesting analogies to be made, and this is the point being made in the blog post, between the kinds of objects we call models in human culture broadly or in science specifically, and the kinds of things people talk about as world models inside language models or other neural sequence models right now.

For example, if you look all the way back to Word2Vec, and before that to LSA-type things, these classical count-based ways of learning word representations by taking the word co-occurrence matrix and finding low-dimensional representations of it, you start to see structure that mirrors somehow the structure of the outside world. There was the famous picture in the Word2Vec paper where you line up all the countries and all the capitals, and there's an approximate east-west axis in one dimension, and there's a country-to-capital relationship in the other direction. Is this a world model? Does Word2Vec have a model of the world? If you're willing to say a globe is a model of the world in the sense that it gives you a low-dimensional representation of the space in which all the countries and their physical relationships live, then it's probably reasonable to talk about Word2Vec, or any of these word embedding models, as having world models of a very, very simple, very noisy form.

items.question: How do you think about language models having world models when their predictions may rely on shallow heuristics?
items.object: Heuristic world models in language models
items.answer:
Coming back to the blog post, the next degree of sophistication above a static map, or static things we talk about as models like model airplanes or model trains, is to think about some sort of system. For example, think about models of celestial mechanics people were working with in the Medieval Era and Renaissance. Even once you figure out the universe is heliocentric, with the sun in the middle and planets moving on rails around the sun, maybe at some fixed distance, you can't necessarily explain why they have the orbits or shapes they have, or why they seem to exist in particular relationships to each other. It takes Newton to give you the complete story. But even without that, you can say, “I have some basic simplified dynamical model of the solar system that lets me say, knowing Mercury is here today and Venus is there today, where they'll be tomorrow, or the next time they'll line up in the same position in the sky.”

I think in fact, when we think about world models in language models, that's the kind of picture we should have in mind most of the time. They don't necessarily understand or have the ability to recapitulate the entire causal process that caused their training data to look the way it does. At the same time, even if it's by way of shallow surface heuristics, they have the ability in distribution to describe what the world looks like today, maybe predict what it will look like tomorrow, and maybe predict what it will look like tomorrow conditioned on some intervention or in a relatively restricted class of counterfactual situations describing other ways the world might have been.

Coming back to whether, if you're using heuristics, it's really a world model: I think there are all kinds of things outside AI that we're happy to call world models that use heuristics with a similar flavor. At some level this is an argument about terminology rather than capabilities.

items.question: How do you think about the boundaries of what you're willing to call a “world model”?
items.object: The scope and boundaries of the term “world model”
items.answer:
Yeah, I'm not sure. There's the world piece of this and the modal piece of this. Even with things that look more explicitly like bottom-up, first-principles physical simulations, we're typically not talking about models of literally the entire world; we're talking about models of specific, narrow domains. Even thinking about the kinds of things referred to as possible worlds in philosophy of language and formal semantics, often the thing you actually imagine you're reasoning about is a description of a situation and not everything in the world.

items.question: How do you think about the question of whether language models represent meaning?
items.object: Whether language models represent meaning
items.answer:
The way we and a lot of people in the NLP community were thinking about it—there was this very influential paper by Bender and Koller about how to conceptualize meaning in language models, which did a very good job of stating that one question we should ask is, “Is a language model a model of meaning, and what would convince us that a language model is a model of meaning?” But the difficulty you immediately run into is that there is no universally agreed-upon definition of what it means to be a model of meaning.

You can give an account really grounded in perception and action: to know the meaning of a word is to know what to do when somebody tells you to do it, to know how to imagine what a scene would look like if it's described to you. There's a whole linguistic tradition that follows in that vein. But you also have abstract model-theoretic notions of meaning that just require some representation of possible worlds that doesn't even necessarily need to ground out in the real world. You have proof-theoretic accounts of meaning that say it suffices to recognize relationships between sentences. There was a huge amount of work in the NLP literature motivated by this, in the form of natural language inference and entailment recognition problems. You can have social causal accounts of meaning that say language derives its meaning from a history of interactions with other people in a kind of community, and so on.

As soon as you start trying to answer the question, “Does a language model represent meaning?” the hard part is the philosophy of language question. As soon as you've made that precise or imported the appropriate terminology from that literature, turning it into a precise question you can ask about a language model becomes relatively easy in most cases. Certainly you can ask: does a language model have the ability to perform entailment? Does it produce representations from which we can reconstruct perceptually grounded representations of situations that are being described? Does it derive its usage of words from the social context in which those words are meaningful?

items.answer:
Well, I think it's more that we now have, for many of the mainstream ways of formulating that question, ways of saying, “Here's a precise test that I would run against the language model to answer this question.” As soon as you do that for any of these formulations, the answer is, “Well, kind of, sometimes.” In that sense, maybe it's not well-posed just to say, “Does it represent meaning? items.question: How do you see the prospects of studying language models internally to answer questions in philosophy of language?
items.object: Mechanistic analysis of language models as a source of philosophical discoveries
items.answer: I am pretty skeptical about the prospects of anything we're doing here answering questions in philosophy of language. I think things flow in the other direction: if you have a theory of how reference works that stands on its own, then you can ask whether that theory is actually implemented in some other model. items.question: What do you think text-trained language models can teach us about the empirical question of acquiring linguistic competence?
items.object: Text-trained language models as evidence about acquiring linguistic competence
items.answer: There are other adjacent questions about how language works that we certainly can learn from studying both how these models work internally and what kind of data they learn from. Just as the empirical question of what kind of data you need to acquire adult-like linguistic competence, for whatever definition you're willing to supply, I think everybody has been surprised that the answer was, “You can do it with a huge amount of text data.” This doesn't tell us definitively how people are acquiring adult-like language competence, and it probably isn't a very similar mechanism. But having all these proofs in principle that if you have enough of this data and a very simple computational architecture, you can build representations with this nice structure and produce outputs reliable to this degree or that degree—these are super interesting and super important scientifically.

items.question: How do you understand the disagreement over whether language models learn models of the world rather than surface correlations?
items.object: Disagreement over whether language models learn world models
items.answer:
I think maybe nobody would ever have disagreed with that as long as people were willing to stake out exactly what degree of faithfulness in that representation was necessary to say, “Yeah, this model is learning to model the world and not just surface correlations.” It basically feels like there's very little disagreement about the empirical facts, and most of the disagreement is about terminology and what you need, either the right definition or useful definition of having meaning or having a world model, and what the acceptable standards of proof are for those things. It's less about whether it's possible that there is literally nothing inside a language model that bears any correspondence to the data-generating process in the outside world.

I think you can still have substantial disagreement about the right degree of fidelity to the underlying process and how faithfully you need to mimic the step-by-step computation it's performing. It's defensible to say your solar system on rails is not actually a model of the solar system because it doesn't know anything about gravity and there's a large category of questions it can't answer.

items.question: How do you understand Deductive Closure Training as a way to help language models learn the implications of their training data?
items.object: Deductive Closure Training and the gap between inference-time reasoning and training-time learning
items.answer:
I should say again that this is an idea that I think has appeared in many forms in the literature over the last few years, if not more than that. There were a bunch of people doing this at inference time, where you say, “Before I answer question X, let me generate everything else I know related to question X and produce my answer in that context.” A couple of papers from AI2 were doing this, and some folks at Stanford. One way to think about what's happening in the DCT paper is just doing it at training time rather than inference time, and observing that you can use it both in a totally unsupervised way and for editing models.

Some folks from Tatsunori Hashimoto's group recently had a paper on synthetic continued pretraining, which is a scaled-up version of a similar idea. Stephen Bach and his lab at Brown have also been doing similar things. I think this has been in the air for a while.

In terms of what comes next, I think there are two important ideas here. One is that different ways of interacting with a language model invoke different, if you want to call them that, world-modeling capabilities, and that there seem to be some available at inference time that aren't available at training time. If I put some fact in the context, models are happy to compute all the implications of that fact. If I take a couple of state steps of gradient descent on text expressing a fact, models memorize the sentence I just trained them on and don't swallow up all the implications. If you want models to derive from their training data everything that's implied by it, you need something like this: some way of turning the ability to do reasoning at inference time into compiling things into the weights at training time. The stuff we're doing here is the very simplest possible form of that.

items.question: What excites you about using reasoning to learn general preferences from human feedback to language models?
items.object: Learning general preference principles from human feedback
items.answer:
One thing I'm really excited about in that direction is, for example, if you're doing live interactions with an individual human user, or collecting preference data to learn from, the same kind of reasoning applies. Even if you're just getting from a user, “I prefer output A to output B,” you can probably distill that into a general principle that explains why this user prefers A to B, or why they prefer the entire set of A's over the entire set of B's. Once you've figured out that general principle, you want to impose it globally on the model.

If you're in a setting where you can collect richer feedback from somebody who's training you, if you're in a robotic setting where you're getting individualized teaching from one person, or even in a normal RLHF setting where you're asking annotators to give richer kinds of annotation to explain their decisions or produce edits, then again you want to extract from those explanations not just “the user prefers A to B,” but a global preference structure: there's some preference being expressed where A is better than any other B I could come up with as long as that explanation is satisfied. Then I think you can use similar techniques to learn from rich supervision that way.

items.question: What do you make of the finding that fine-tuning a model on true sentences improves its ability to verify unrelated facts?
items.object: Fine-tuning on true sentences improving verification of unrelated facts
items.answer: One thing that's been found many times that I still find very spooky is that you take a model, fine-tune it on a bunch of sentences that are true, and it gets better at doing fact verification about totally unrelated facts. Somewhere latently in this model, there's some notion or ability to perform this task that is not maximally activated or that's having to compete with other things when you get your even supervised fine-tuned model off the shelf. I think we still have a lot to figure out about what is happening in those cases. Until we figured it out, we have these external behavioral synthetic data generation things that we can do instead.

items.question: How do you see academia's role in developing a scientific understanding of language models?
items.object: Academia's role in developing a scientific understanding of language models
items.answer:
In terms of the role for academia, I think we're in this funny state that almost feels like being a 19th-century natural scientist, where we have big, complicated systems we don't totally understand. We're in a kind of pre-theoretical state, and there's a huge amount of work to be done both on figuring out concrete things about how they work and even what it means to do good science here, or the terms by which we recognize a good, useful predictive theory of LLM behavior. This is something academia is extremely well positioned to explore. We have pretty big open models; it doesn't require huge computational resources to hold them in your hands and look at what they're doing when processing a single document.

Even in a world where it turns out not to be necessary to have any of that scientific understanding to build tomorrow's language models, I think it's incredibly interesting in its own right, as another window into the nature of intelligence, reasoning, and thought, and how close you can get to the things we give those names in human cognition in this very alien system produced in a different way that works in a very different way.

items.question: How do you frame research questions about language models so they remain interesting as implementations change?
items.object: Designing lasting research questions about language models
items.answer:
A strategy that has worked surprisingly well, at least for the questions we're interested in, is to think of this thing as a black box that's someday going to be as good as possible at doing what it does right now. What are the research questions that are still interesting to ask that aren't tied to specific implementation decisions people are making today?

In the context of interpretability work, what kinds of questions can you ask about interpretability without saying “Transformer,” without saying “RNN,” or, to the greatest extent possible, without saying “neural”? Can you frame these as general questions about complex systems that do language generation? The kinds of things that have stood up are asking what the right question is, what the right data set is for asking it, or what experiment you can design that is sufficiently general that you can do it without knowing there's such a thing as an attention head or feed-forward layer inside an underlying model.

items.question: What have you come to value in good science through drawing on research from other fields?
items.object: Good science and its value across fields
items.answer: With regard to the broader question of what good science looks like in general, I don't know. The work we've done that I'm most excited about has often come not from reading a bunch of papers that appeared in CS or CS/ML in the last week, but by looking at other fields: formal semantics, or recently thinking about state tracking in the context of what we know about how to compute operations on groups in a more general way, or what we know about how to ask people good questions. From that perspective, as a user of good science in other fields, I think it really is saying the kinds of things likely to be legible, meaningful, and influential to people working in totally different areas.
